citeAs: Masry, A., Long, D. X., Tan, J. Q., Joty, S., and Hoque, E. (2022). ChartQA: A Benchmark for Question Answering about Charts with Visual and Logical Reasoning. arXiv:2203.10244.
creator: Ahmed Masry, Do Xuan Long, Jia Qing Tan, Shafiq Joty, Enamul Hoque (York University, Canada; Nanyang Technological University, Singapore; Salesforce Research)
description: ChartQA is a large-scale benchmark for question answering about charts with visual and logical reasoning. It covers 9,608 human-written questions (ChartQA-H) and 23,111 machine-generated questions from human-written chart summaries (ChartQA-M), spanning 20,882 real-world charts from four online sources (Statista, Pew Research, Our World In Data, and OECD). The benchmark focuses on compositional and visual reasoning questions involving arithmetic and logical operations over bar, line, and pie charts.
name: ChartQA
rai:annotationsPerItem: 2 questions per chart (each answered by two annotators independently for validation)
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Inter-annotator agreement based on exact match was 61.04%. A manual check on 500 random samples found agreement of 78.55% when accounting for typos and lexical variations (e.g., "3$" vs "3 dollars", "86.33" vs "86.3"). For machine-generated questions, manual analysis of 1,250 QA pairs found that 86.64% were complete, answerable, and correct given the chart.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: For human-authored QA pairs (ChartQA-H): Workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk were asked to provide two questions per chart image, focusing on (1) compositional questions (containing at least two mathematical/logical operations like sum, difference, average) and (2) visual questions (referring to visual attributes such as color, height, length of graphical marks). For each chart, workers provided two questions with answers. The same questions were then answered by another annotator. If both workers' answers exactly matched, the answer was considered correct; otherwise, answers were manually checked. Workers were required to have an acceptance rate of 95% and at least 5,000 accomplished HITs, and passed a pre-test for qualification. For machine-generated QA pairs (ChartQA-M): A T5 model was fine-tuned on SQuAD and applied to human-written Statista chart summaries to generate questions. Invalid questions were filtered using a heuristic (answer must be found in the chart data table), and the test set was manually cleaned.
rai:dataBiases: Politics is a common topic across all sources, particularly in the Pew dataset where nearly half of charts are about U.S. Politics & Policy (45.4%). Bar charts are the most common chart type across all datasets. Among bar charts, 79.4% were simple and 29.6% were complex; for line charts, 61.0% were simple and 39.0% were complex. The machine-generated questions (ChartQA-M) may contain invalid or unanswerable questions due to domain mismatch between training (SQuAD) and test (chart summaries) domains; manual checking found ~24% noise in heuristic-based supervision for difference/ratio operations.
rai:dataCollection: Charts were crawled from four online sources: (1) Statista (statista.com), an online platform covering economy, politics, and industry; (2) Pew Research (pewresearch.org), publishing reports on social and economic issues; (3) Our World In Data or OWID (ourworldindata.org), covering global issues; and (4) OECD (oecd.org), sharing reports for policymaking. For Pew, only chart images were crawled (no underlying data tables). For the other three, underlying data tables, metadata (e.g., title, chart type), SVG files, and associated text descriptions were extracted. Bounding box information of chart elements was extracted from SVG files. Human-authored QA pairs were collected via Amazon Mechanical Turk, and additional QA pairs were generated from human-written Statista chart summaries using a fine-tuned T5 model.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Real-world chart images from Statista, Pew Research, Our World In Data (OWID), and OECD. For Statista, OWID, and OECD, underlying data tables, metadata (title, chart type), SVG files, and associated text descriptions were also collected. For Pew, only chart images were available. Charts include bar, line, and pie chart types.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, Web API
rai:dataLimitations: Models perform worse when the gold data table is not provided, highlighting challenges in automatic data extraction from real-world charts with diverse styles. Current approaches for automatic data extraction are modular and error-prone, especially for pie charts and charts with logarithmic scales or very large values. The T5 question generation model may generate invalid or unanswerable questions due to training/test domain mismatch. Evaluation metrics for chart data extraction do not account for extracted textual tokens, which are noisier in real-world figures. Models cannot guarantee correct output and may be abused to mislead the public.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Dataset augmentation was performed by generating 23,111 questions from human-written Statista chart summaries using a fine-tuned T5 model (ChartQA-M), to supplement the 9,608 human-authored questions (ChartQA-H). Both datasets were randomly split into train, validation, and test sets.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For ChartQA-M (machine-generated): A heuristic filter was applied to remove invalid questions where the answer could not be found in the chart data table. The test set was additionally manually cleaned by removing invalid questions. For chart data extraction: ChartOCR was extended to extract fully-structured data tables from chart images, using key-point detection networks, CRAFT model for text recognition, and color/proximity heuristics to associate data values with text labels. Data was randomly split into train, validation, and test sets for both ChartQA-H and ChartQA-M.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The models trained on this dataset can be abused to mislead the public about chart content and implications. The dataset was collected respecting intellectual property rights of sources (Statista, Pew, OECD, OWID), using only publicly available charts that comply with their terms and conditions. Annotators were compensated at or above the US minimum wage ($7.25/hour), receiving $0.60 per task (estimated 3-5 minutes each). Annotator annotations were anonymized to protect privacy.
rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking chart question answering (ChartQA) systems that involve visual and logical reasoning over real-world charts. Intended to serve as a starting point for developing models that can answer complex compositional and visual reasoning questions about bar, line, and pie charts.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: T5 model (fine-tuned on SQuAD) used for answer extraction and answer-aware question generation to produce ChartQA-M questions from human-written Statista summaries. ChartOCR (Luo et al., 2021) extended for automatic chart data extraction. CRAFT model (Baek et al., 2019) for text recognition in chart elements.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Annotator annotations were anonymized to protect the privacy of Amazon Mechanical Turk workers. No personal or sensitive information about individuals is collected in the dataset itself (charts cover topics like economy, politics, health, and society at aggregate/statistical level).
